results.ask: Thinking about the book as a whole, what does this opening promise a reader?
results.watch: Stays at the whole; no sentence edits or line suggestions; any other level only as a closing choice.
results.reply:
At the level of the whole book, this opening makes a few promises I can see in these exact words.

The clearest one is a book about what people don't say. Mara won't cry; Tomas gets "In a minute" instead of anything true; even the gulls "kept their own counsel." That last line extends the withholding to the world itself — the narration is willing to treat the landscape as something that knows and declines to tell. A reader who takes that in may expect a book where information arrives late, sideways, or not at all, and where the pressure comes from what's being held rather than what's happening.

The second promise is about who the story belongs to. We're with Mara for almost all of it, but one clause steps into Tomas: he "thought she was being ridiculous." That's doing two possible jobs at once, and the passage doesn't settle which. Either the narration can go into anyone's head whenever it likes, or Mara is assuming what he thinks and the narration is staying with her. Both are workable promises, but they're different books. The first says you'll be given more than any one character knows. The second says you'll be locked inside a woman who reads dismissal into the man beside her, and that her reading may or may not be right. Whichever you intend, a reader will take an impression of it from this sentence, because it's the only place in the passage where the vantage point moves.

Third: speech here isn't set apart from the rest. "You coming, he said" sits in the same flow as the pewter water and the gulls. That promises a book where talking is one more thing that occurs, no louder than weather — not a book of scenes built on dialogue.

And then the actual engine. The last sentence is the only one that reaches toward something: she can still see the coat at the rail. That's the question the opening hands a reader to carry — who is leaving, what he is to her, why she is standing on a dock with Tomas instead of on that boat. The passage establishes that she's watching a man go and won't say so. Everything beyond that is mine to guess, which is likely the point.

What I'd want before saying anything about whether these are the promises you want to make: whether the man at the rail stays in the book or is gone after this, and whether Tomas is a presence throughout or a figure from this one morning. The opening's promises are only keepable or breakable against what actually follows.

results.reply:
Working at the level of how the scene is shaped — where it opens and what it withholds.

What strikes me first: the scene opens after the parting. The ferry is already pulling away, so the goodbye, the walk to the dock, whatever was said — all of that sits behind the first line. What the opening gives us instead is the aftermath, a woman holding herself together on a dock. That's a real choice and it does something: the pressure in the passage comes from what Mara won't do rather than from anything happening.

The thing I'd want you to look at is the last sentence. "She could still see the color of his coat at the rail" is the first time we learn there's a third person — someone on that boat. Until then the ferry is just a ferry, and Tomas is the only other person present. So the reader spends six sentences not knowing what the scene is about, and then finds out in the final clause. That can work as a held breath, the reveal landing like a confession she's been avoiding. It can also mean a reader is reading the early lines without the thing that would make them ache.

One other thing worth naming, since it bears on where the scene is anchored: "thought she was being ridiculous" steps into Tomas for a moment. Everything else sits with Mara. If the scene is hers, that half-line is a small window into someone else's head, and it's doing something — it makes her alone in a sharper way — but it's worth knowing whether you meant it.

Before I'd suggest moving anything, I'd need to know what comes before this. If the reader already knows who's on that boat, the last line is a return and the withholding isn't really withholding. If this is the first we hear of him, the shape of the scene is quite different and the question of where to start is a live one.

results.ask: Does this scene start in the right place?

results.reply:
At the level of scene shape: the passage opens after the decisive action. The ferry is already pulling away, so nothing happens on the page except waiting, withholding, and being summoned. That's a coherent choice — it puts the weight on what Mara is holding rather than on an event — but it means the first five sentences ask a reader to watch someone watch, without yet knowing what she's watching.

The thing that orients us arrives last: *his coat at the rail*. Until that sentence, the ferry is just a ferry. So the scene currently starts at the moment of aftermath and withholds the stake until the closing beat.

Two directions, neither better than the other:

Keep it as is, and the last line lands as a quiet reveal — the reader rereads the whole paragraph with a person in it. The cost is that some readers may spend the early lines unanchored, which also mutes Tomas's impatience, since we don't yet know what she's refusing to leave.

Or let the reader know earlier that someone is aboard, and start closer to the goodbye itself — perhaps the boarding, or the last thing said. That gains pressure on *She would not cry, not here*, because we'd know what she's not crying about. The cost is real: you'd lose the deferred recognition, and the paragraph currently ends on sight, which is a stronger close than ending on the gulls would be.

Worth saying that *The gulls kept their own counsel* is doing something the rest of the passage doesn't — it's the one line with a point of view outside Mara's, and it's dry in a way that keeps the scene from tipping into sentiment. Whatever you do with the opening, that line seems load-bearing.

It's arguing that a familiar idea rests on shakier ground than people think — and notice it stops short of saying the idea is wrong. The strongest claim in the words themselves is "far less tidy," which casts doubt without replacing the belief with anything.

Two things I notice about how the argument is aimed. "Seemed to prove it" in the second sentence already signals where you're going, so the third sentence lands as confirmation rather than as news. And the target shifts: you open with what most of us believe, and close by holding the bestsellers responsible for the tidiness. The paragraph doesn't say whether the reader should now stop believing the muscle idea, or just stop trusting the books that sold it. Both are available readings of these words; the passage doesn't settle which.

Whether that openness is a problem depends on what comes next — if the following paragraphs resolve it, the hold here may be deliberate.

results.reply:
In plain terms: the paragraph isn't arguing that willpower *isn't* like a muscle. It's arguing that we don't have the grounds to be as sure of that as we've been told. The belief stands in the first sentence, the support arrives in the second, and the third pulls the support out without touching the belief itself — so what you end on is a claim about the state of the evidence, and about the gap between that evidence and "the bestsellers."

The thing doing most of the work is how carefully the verbs stay smaller than the thing they're correcting. "Seemed to prove" grants the studies their moment without conceding the point. "Have failed" reports what happened to the replications rather than ruling on willpower. "Far less tidy" describes the shape of a picture instead of announcing a conclusion. The effect is that the paragraph can unsettle a confident claim while making almost no confident claim of its own — the only flat assertion in it is that attempts to repeat the results have failed.
